title: Copying Armstrong's When You're Smiling; high notes and rhythm notation
summary: He spent a summer transcribing Armstrong, played to high G because he did not know it was a limit, and learned to write Armstrong's phrasing in double time.

story.theme_name: Working with and around Louis Armstrong
story.community_name: Playing with and around Louis Armstrong

blocks.x: The first ARmstrong record I ever copied was "When You're Smiling," which goes up to a high E on the trumpet. In those days if the trumpet player could play up to a high C they thought it was pretty phenomenal. So it was kind of lucky for me that I listened to Louis Armstrong. I didn't know that the trumpet was supposed to stop at C so when I was in high school I could play up to high G. Because it's a matter of your attitude, how high you play, basically. You know, just as young guys come along now, they think in terms of double high C. Well, I don't think that high so any notes above G, I can't
tell you what they are if I hear them. But, you know, the younger players, many of them think high. They listen to Cat Anderson, Maynard Ferguson.

I was just wondering, that was pretty advanced to be able to copy. Most youngsters couldn't copy those things. You must have had an extremely good ear and a lot of patience to keep playing this record over again.

Well, I'm very stubborn. And I would sit -- it was the summertime. I spent the whole summer just trying to copy this three minutes of music. And maybe four or five hours a day. And it would just take each instrument one note at a time and write them down. And I'd go back over it and try to figure out the rhythmic pattern. And that was what gave me the most trouble.

It gave me the most trouble on Louis Armstrong solos, trying to write those out, until it dawned on me that when he played he thought in eight. And if you write it out as in double time, then it's perfectly clear. But when I was young I tried to write them out in eighths, I'd say, "rush" or "slow down" instead of writing the 16ths in there that I should have written.
Well, I don't know how interesting it is.
